schools.summary: Henry marks the change from covenanting by blood-sacrifice at Sinai to sealing written articles, orders the four ranks (governor, priests, Levites, chiefs), and reads Ezra's absence as leaving others their part after his work as scribe.

Clarke lays down the four sealing classes and wonders that neither Ezra, Eliashib, nor any prophet appears; Wesley has them subscribe in their own and all the people's names, Ezra kept away by sickness or impediment (cf. Neh. 12:36).
Ellicott takes Zidkijah for Zadok the scribe, Nehemiah's secretary (Neh. 13:13; cf. Ezra 4:8).
Gill notes simply that those who sealed were the persons named following.

debates.question: Why is Ezra absent from the list of those who sealed?

sides.position: prevented by sickness or some extraordinary impediment
having done his part as a scribe at the reading of the law, he left it to others to do theirs

themes: a written renewal of an old duty

schools.summary: Ellicott weighs 'all they that had separated themselves' — not a recognised body of proselytes but the descendants of Israelites left in the land (cf. Neh. 9:2), the covenant mindful of the danger from commerce with the heathen; the children of understanding included in the oath.
Clarke: all the people were bound through their representatives in the classes that sealed, as truly as if each had signed.
Gill takes 'the rest of the people' for those who did not themselves sign and seal.

themes: separated unto the law of God
a covenant reaching every rank and age

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render 'holding with,' distinguish the community from the princes and heads of orders, and read the newly joined as Israelites left in the land; Ellicott weighs the oath (assuming the obligation) and the curse (imprecating the penalty), cf. Deut. 29:12.
Wesley dwells on the nobles called brethren, rich and poor meeting in the things of God; Clarke: the unsealed bound themselves by solemn oath to walk according to the law of Moses.
Gill reads the cleaving as ratifying assent to what the nobles had sealed.
Keil and Delitzsch set the refusal of heathen marriage at the head of the covenant's several engagements, the first way that had to be shut if the community would walk by God's law.
Gill: the people had been guilty of this and were prone to it still, the guilt owned at Ezra 9:2 — the door by which idolatry entered.
Clarke glosses the vow as making 'no affinity with the people of the land.'

themes: striking first at the besetting sin

schools.summary: Ellicott extends the rule to the holy days, reads 'leave the seventh year' of the untilled ground, and 'the exaction of every debt' as the Lord's release of Deut. 15:2.
Clarke gathers both vows — solemnly keep the sabbath, let the land rest every seventh year (Exod. 23:10-11); Wesley warns the profanation of the sabbath is a sure inlet to all profaneness.
Gill glosses the 'ware' as any goods brought to be sold on the holy day.

themes: the sabbath the gate against profaneness

schools.summary: Henry marks the turn from ceasing evil to learning to do well: a self-imposed levy to furnish God's table, the people charging themselves, and no blessing to be looked for where public worship is not maintained.
Clarke explains the third-shekel (against the law's half of Exod. 30:13) by their poverty, the half resumed in prosperity as the didrachma of Matt. 17:24 shows.
Ellicott reads it the origin of the annual temple-rate later raised to a half shekel, the ancient half having been only an occasional tax.
Gill: they made an ordinance for themselves, binding themselves to what the written law had not required.

Keil and Delitzsch fix 'we laid upon ourselves' as a revival of Exod. 30:13 (still paid in Christ's day, Matt. 17:24), lowered to a third for poverty, and 'the service of the house' as the regular worship, not the building — rejecting Aben Ezra's 'third in addition.'
Gill reads it as defraying the constant expense, beginning with the shewbread.
Henry itemizes the daily and festal offerings and presses that worship worth keeping is worth paying for.

Keil and Delitzsch note the law required the altar's standing fire (Lev. 6:12) but gave no rule for procuring wood, so the rulers must provide it; Ellicott sees here the origin of the feast of the wood-offering, the lot ordering the classes.
Clarke: the wood had been the Nethinim's charge, but few returned, so districts brought it by lot in turn — later the feast Xylophoria named by Josephus, though not in Scripture.
Gill notes priests and Levites in one lot, the people in another.
Ellicott reads the firstfruits following the covenant's 'we made ordinances,' the minute specification implying that neglect had crept in.
Gill: not cast by lot as the wood but bound by oath per the law; Aben Ezra would restrict it to the sheaf and the two wave-loaves.
Henry gathers firstfruits and tithes as the ministers' maintenance, the withholding of which is the robbing of God charged in Mal. 3:8.

themes: detail as a sign of past neglect
the first and best given to God

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch trace each due to its statute (Exod. 23:19; Num. 18:13, 16, 17); Ellicott sharpens the distinction — sons and unclean cattle redeemed by valuation, clean firstlings brought for sacrifice.
Gill distinguishes the firstborn of sons and unclean cattle (redeemed) from the clean firstlings (offered).
Clarke grounds the law in Exod. 13:2 — the Levites taken in the room of Israel's firstborn.

themes: the Levites as ransom of the firstborn

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch lay out the flow of dues — firstfruits and heave-offerings to the priests' chambers, the tithe of the ground to the Levites in the country towns; Ellicott identifies the store-chambers (1 Kings 6; Hezekiah's treasure-house, 2 Chron. 31:11) and the cities of tillage.
Gill notes the first of the dough brought per the law, a cake set apart for the priest.

themes: firstfruits of dough and the tithes

schools.summary: Ellicott sends the reader to Num. 18:22-26 for the distinction of priest and Levite, the priest present when tithes were gathered in the Levitical cities to secure the tithe of the tithe.
Clarke explains the 'tithe of the tithes' — the tenth the Levites gave the priests out of the tithe they received (Num. 18:26).
Gill reads the priest's presence as a safeguard against defrauding the priests of their due.

themes: honest handling of the sanctuary's revenue

schools.summary: Clarke swells 'we will not forsake the house of our God' into a meditation — the Church the house of God, believers his family, ministers its officers, ordinances its food — those who forsake it not continue in faith, grow, labour, and maintain its offerings.
Ellicott notes the priests exempt from gathering the tithes, and that the pledge and its breach are alike explained by Neh. 13:11-14.
Gill reads the offerings of corn, wine, and oil flowing to the temple chambers.

themes: we will not forsake the house of our God
the pledge and its later breach
to forsake the house is to forsake God

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe the written amanah, a sure agreement built 'upon all this' preceding penitence and sealed by the heads of houses (the word recurs at Neh. 11:23); Ellicott takes Seraiah for the high-priestly house of Ezra and Eliashib, one of whom — probably Ezra — sealed for it.
Keil and Delitzsch treat the priestly names as the courses of the return (cf. Ezra 2:36ff.), heads of houses each standing for his order, kept in their ranks for exactness.
Henry numbers the priests at twenty-two, next after the governor, the teachers of the law foremost in binding themselves to keep it.
Clarke reckons the priests the second sealing class (vv. 2-8) and marvels that neither Ezra nor Eliashib appears.

Keil and Delitzsch place the Levites among some fourteen heads of houses and pass to the forty-four chiefs (thirteen from Zerubbabel's kindreds, cf. Ezra 2), the greater number laid to the growth of the houses; Ellicott finds the family names traceable in the earlier lists.
Henry reckons seventeen Levites, most of them the mouth of the congregation in the prayer of Neh. 9:4-5 — those who lead in prayer should lead in every good work.
Clarke keeps them in the third sealing class, the Levites between priests and chiefs.

themes: the roll turning to the chiefs
those who lead in prayer lead in the covenant

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch keep these among the forty-four lay heads and note the roll opens at once into the accession of all the community — priests, Levites, porters, singers, Nethinim, and people; Ellicott finds the names personal, familial, and local.
Henry sees the heads of Neh. 7:8 reappearing here, subscribing for their fathers' houses, their names set on record to their honour.
Clarke keeps them in the fourth sealing class, the chief of the people (vv. 14-27).

themes: the people's accession to the covenant
names on record to their honour

schools.summary: Ellicott reads 'these were the priests' as naming the priestly families (cf. Neh. 12:1-6); Keil and Delitzsch count these among the one-and-twenty names of the returning courses, the orders kept distinct.
Henry numbers the priests at twenty-two, set next after the governor as teachers of the law.
Clarke joins the standing wonder that neither Ezra nor Eliashib is among them.

Ellicott finds several Levitical family names traceable in the return (Ezra 2:40); Keil and Delitzsch reckon fourteen Levites led by Jeshua, Binnui, and Kadmiel (who returned with seventy-four others and appear as heads of orders in Neh. 12:8).
Henry reckons seventeen Levites, most of them the mouth of the congregation in the prayer of Neh. 9:4-5.
Clarke sets them in the third sealing class, following the priests.

themes: those who led the confession lead the pledge

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the names as personal, familial, and local, the houses multiplied since Ezra 2; Keil and Delitzsch count forty-four heads, thirteen from Zerubbabel's kindreds, the rest heads of houses or elders of the smaller towns.
Henry sees the heads of Neh. 7:8 among the first of the chief of the people to seal, subscribing for their fathers' houses.
Clarke sets them in the fourth sealing class, filling the register to v. 27.

themes: the great clans of the return

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch reckon these among the one-and-twenty priestly names, heads of returning courses kept in their ranks; Ellicott reads them as family names to be compared with Neh. 12:1-6.
Henry numbers the priests at twenty-two, the teachers of the law foremost in the subscription.
Clarke sets them in the second sealing class (vv. 2-8) and wonders that neither Ezra nor Eliashib appears.

themes: the teachers first at the covenant

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch count fourteen Levites headed by Jeshua, Binnui, and Kadmiel (who returned with seventy-four others, Neh. 7:43, and appear as heads of orders in Neh. 12:8); Ellicott finds the family names traceable at Ezra 2:40.
Henry reckons seventeen Levites, most of them the mouth of the congregation in the prayer of Neh. 9:4-5.
Clarke places them in the third sealing class (vv. 9-13).

themes: those who prayed lead in pledging
the singers of penitence pledge amendment

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch reckon forty-four lay heads, thirteen from Zerubbabel's kindreds (Ezra 2), the rest heads of branched houses or elders of the smaller towns, the larger number laid to the growth of the community; Ellicott reads the names as personal, familial, and local.
Henry: they gave it under their hands for themselves and all the rest, their names left on record to their honour.
Clarke sets them in the fourth sealing class (vv. 14-27).

themes: the representative weight of the seal

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the forty-four heads to include both the ancient kindreds and the newer houses, with the elders of the lesser towns of Judah and Benjamin (not every name in the older list of Ezra 2); Ellicott reads them as personal, familial, and local.
Henry: a great thing when men of influence throw it on the side of religion, these chief men subscribing for all they could sway, their names on record to their honour.
Clarke keeps them in the last sealing class, the roll ending with Baanah in v. 27.

themes: every rank bound through its heads
the elders of the smallest towns
the covenant as wide as Israel
